name: Outdoor Advertising
description: Outdoor advertising in Iran brings commercial messages into streets and other shared urban spaces. Tehran provides documented examples of how municipal advertising structures, licensed agencies, content approval, and cultural programming intersect.

seo.title: Outdoor Advertising in Iran: Billboards and Urban Space
seo.description: Explore Tehran’s documented billboard arrangements, the distinction between site operation and content approval, and the use of advertising spaces for art.

content.heading: A medium embedded in the city
content.content:
In Tehran, billboards form part of a shared visual environment containing commercial advertising alongside political, religious, and public messages. Research by Narciss Sohrabi and Negar Zojaji describes these parallel functions and examines a temporary intervention that replaced familiar messages with artworks. Their study frames billboards as part of the relationship between citizens and urban images, rather than simply as surfaces rented by advertisers. [s1]

This distinction helps international readers interpret what they encounter. A large roadside image is not necessarily a commercial placement, and its visibility does not establish whether anyone paid for it. The documented coexistence of different kinds of messages means that an account of outdoor advertising must consider who controls the surface, who supplies the message, and what purpose the display serves. [s1]

content.heading: Site operation and content approval
content.content:
A September 2019 report published by Tasnim quoted Hamid Saber Farzam, then an advertising and revenue official at Tehran’s Beautification Organization, describing separate responsibilities. According to his account, municipal advertising structures were allocated to advertising agencies licensed by the Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance, the national ministry responsible for relevant cultural licensing. Advertising designs required ministry approval before display. [s2]

The official also described a municipal role in checking whether the version submitted for installation matched the approved design. His account therefore distinguished content approval from administration of the advertising structures; it did not describe an absence of municipal involvement. [s2]

This is a dated institutional explanation, not a verified statement of the complete rules in force in October 2026. It also concerns Tehran’s municipal structures. It cannot establish arrangements for every privately controlled surface, transport facility, or municipality elsewhere in Iran. Contemporary procurement documents and local regulations are needed before extending this model to other settings. [s2]

content.heading: When advertising spaces became an exhibition
content.content:
In May 2015, Tehran temporarily displayed reproductions of Iranian and international artworks on billboards normally carrying other messages. A Reuters report carried by Ynet described the project as an open-air exhibition and recorded both appreciation and criticism. The intervention demonstrates that advertising infrastructure can also become a vehicle for cultural programming. [s3]

Sohrabi and Zojaji’s article identifies the initiative as a change in the city’s usual billboard landscape and states that it generated debate among citizens and experts. Only the article’s abstract was inspected for this page, so no detailed findings about audience responses are attributed to the study. [s1]

The event should not be treated as proof of a lasting change in commercial advertising policy or increased museum attendance. The reporting establishes that the display occurred; it does not establish its subsequent cultural or economic effects. Understanding outdoor advertising in Iran therefore requires keeping the physical display, its institutional arrangements, and evidence of audience response distinct. [s1][s3]

name: Advertising Effectiveness
description: Advertising effectiveness concerns the additional outcomes advertising causes, rather than the activity a reporting system associates with it. In Iran, evaluating those outcomes also requires attention to disruptions that can affect both customer access and the evidence available to analysts.

seo.title: Advertising Effectiveness in Iran: Measurement and Evidence
seo.description: Understand attribution, incremental impact, experiments, and the evidence needed to assess advertising results in Iran.

content.heading: What did advertising actually change?
content.content:
An advertisement can receive a click shortly before a purchase without having caused that purchase. The central question in effectiveness research is what customers would have done without the advertising. Randall Lewis, Justin Rao, and David Reiley’s research overview distinguishes the abundance of digital reporting metrics from the harder task of measuring causal effects on consumer behavior. Its abstract supports that methodological distinction; detailed findings from the full paper are not asserted here. [s1]

A useful evaluation therefore begins with a defined outcome and period. Reporting exposure, visits, or transactions answers different questions from estimating additional purchases. Treating these as interchangeable can make a campaign appear successful merely because it reached people who were already likely to buy. [s1][s2]

content.heading: Three complementary approaches
content.content:
Google’s media effectiveness guide distinguishes attribution, incrementality experiments, and marketing mix modelling. Attribution assigns credit among recorded interactions on a conversion path. It can support frequent campaign decisions, but assigning credit does not itself establish causation. [s2]

Incrementality experiments compare outcomes between groups assigned to receive advertising and groups from which it is withheld. Marketing mix modelling instead uses aggregate information to examine media investment alongside other influences on sales, including seasonality, prices, and economic conditions. The guide presents the methods as complementary and acknowledges limitations: experiments concern particular strategies and periods, while models depend on assumptions and suitable data. Google sells advertising, so this is a vendor-authored methodological guide rather than independent evidence of results in Iran. [s2]

An eBay field-experiment abstract provides a concrete warning about selection. Tom Blake, Chris Nosko, and Steven Tadelis reported that conventional estimates overstated paid-search returns and that responses differed between customer groups. These findings concern the studied eBay campaigns; they do not establish the returns of Iranian search advertising or imply that every brand campaign is ineffective. [s3]

content.heading: Why the Iranian operating context matters
content.content:
Reporting from Iran illustrates why changes in access belong in a campaign’s evidence record. In January 2026, Associated Press described an internet shutdown disrupting businesses that depended on online advertising and communication with customers. Interviewees reported difficulty reaching audiences on the services they normally used. These accounts document disruption, not a representative estimate of advertising returns. [s4]

The measurement implication is an inference: a fall in recorded visits during an outage cannot automatically be attributed to weaker advertising. Both the route to the customer and the route by which activity is measured may have changed. An evaluation should establish which services were accessible before comparing periods. [s4]

content.heading: Reading results with appropriate confidence
content.content:
A credible effectiveness claim identifies the outcome, explains the comparison, and states what the method cannot resolve. Attribution reports, aggregate models, and experiments should retain their different meanings when summarized for readers. Evidence from another country can explain a method without supplying an Iranian benchmark. [s1][s2][s3]

No inspected source establishes a representative annual Iranian effectiveness series. The defensible conclusion is methodological: more detailed reporting can improve description, but a claim of additional impact still requires a justified causal comparison. [s1][s2]

name: Digital Publishing
description: Digital publishing connects editorial work with electronic formats, distribution platforms, and reading or listening software. Iranian services such as Taaghche and Fidibo illustrate how Persian-language books, audio, and periodicals reach audiences through platform-mediated access.

seo.title: Digital Publishing in Iran: Formats, Platforms and Access
seo.description: Explore Persian digital books, audiobooks, magazines, publishing platforms, and the distinction between content production and reader access.

content.heading: From an edited work to a usable publication
content.content:
Digital publishing involves more than placing a document online. Taaghche, an Iranian reading and listening platform, describes its role as connecting publishers with readers while preparing supplied content for digital use. Its account separates the publisher’s work from platform tasks such as technical optimization, presentation, discovery, and reader experience. This is the company’s description of its own workflow, rather than an independently audited account of the whole industry. [s1]

That distinction provides a useful introduction to the field. Editorial production determines the work being published; technical preparation determines how it can be read or heard; distribution determines how an audience obtains access. A weakness at any stage can limit the usefulness of the finished publication. The platform’s account shows why digital distribution still depends on coordination with publishers. [s1]

content.heading: Books, audio, and periodicals serve different needs
content.content:
Taaghche’s frequently asked questions distinguish EPUB books from PDF publications. EPUB is used for text that can adapt to the reading screen, whereas PDF preserves a page arrangement. The service explains that preserving layout matters for many magazines and newspapers. This makes the choice of format an editorial and usability decision: continuous prose and a carefully composed magazine spread do not necessarily benefit from the same presentation. [s2]

Fidibo, another Iranian digital reading service, lists electronic books, audiobooks, magazines, and podcasts within its offering. These categories show that a publishing platform may distribute both written and spoken material. They do not make all audio equivalent: an audiobook and a podcast remain distinct editorial forms even when a service offers both. [s3]

The practical question for a reader is therefore what the particular edition provides. A platform’s broad catalogue description cannot establish the format, navigation, or availability of every title. [s2][s3]

content.heading: Persian reading requires deliberate technical preparation
content.content:
EPUB supports an explicit right-to-left page progression setting. The W3C specification distinguishes that publication-level progression from direction and presentation within individual content documents. For Persian publishing, this means that choosing a supported file format is only the beginning: reading order and local layout still need to be prepared and checked. [s4]

Accessibility is another separate concern. The specification connects EPUB accessibility with web accessibility principles and a dedicated EPUB accessibility specification. A publication’s digital existence therefore does not, by itself, establish that it works well with assistive technology. These standards describe technical capabilities and requirements; they do not certify that the Iranian platforms or individual editions discussed here implement them fully. [s4]

content.heading: Publishing relationships and reader access
content.content:
Taaghche’s published terms say that it contracts with licensed publishers and requires the relevant permissions for supplied content. Authors, translators, and narrators wishing to publish through the service are directed to work through a publisher rather than contract directly with the platform. This documents one service’s stated participation model; it should not be generalized into a universal description of Iranian digital publishing. [s5]

The same terms distinguish access within the service from unrestricted possession of a transferable file. Purchased books are described as remaining in the account archive, while use is restricted to Taaghche’s reading applications. The terms also describe downloading for offline reading. Offline access and permission to redistribute a file are consequently different matters. [s5]

Fidibo describes both individual purchases and its FidiPlus subscription offering. A purchase model and a subscription model are different routes to access; neither description alone establishes that every title is included under identical conditions. [s3]

content.heading: Exploring the field
content.content:
The branches of this section follow different parts of the publishing process. E-books, audiobooks, and digital magazines concern publication forms. Content publishing platforms concern distribution and access. Translation services and writing tools concern work that contributes to preparing content. This division follows the site’s taxonomy and should not be read as a claim that each branch has the same commercial structure.

The inspected services offer concrete entry points into Persian digital publishing, but their descriptions are not a census. Platform catalogue totals would need dates, definitions, and treatment of duplicate editions before they could support national comparisons. The most useful starting point is the particular work and edition: its format, publisher, access conditions, and reading or listening experience. [s1][s2][s3][s5]
